newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss plan gold sales to launch humanitarian fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss plan gold sales to launch humanitarian fund.

text.p: Swiss President Arnold Koller proposed on Wednesday creating a huge humanitarian fund that would sell some of the country's official gold reserves to aid victims of human rights abuses, catastrophes and the Holocaust.

In a major address to parliament on Switzerland's role as a World War Two financial centre, Koller said the planned "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" underscored the Swiss humanitarian tradition and gratitude for having escaped two world wars.
Switzerland's Jewish community and bankers welcomed the surprise idea, but a top right-wing politician blasted it as a misguided giveaway of state wealth in response to international pressure.
Gold prices dipped on fears the sales would hit the market.

But analysts noted any sales would have to wait around two years while Berne moved a legal framework for the foundation through the slow Swiss legislative process -- with the danger of further delay if opponents mount a referendum drive to block it.
Swiss Jews savoured the idea of using Swiss gold, a magnet for vicious volleys of foreign criticism, for humanitarian ends.
"I found it very courageous of Mr Koller to announce this. In principle we are positive about such a foundation," said Swiss Jewish Federation Vice President Thomas Lyssy.
"If you can use Swiss gold for something positive, then you should do it," he said, but added he needed more details.
But right-wing politician Christoph Blocher, who has led a fight against using Swiss public funds to help compensate Hitler's victims for wartime suffering, was aghast.
"The federal council has lost its head," he told Swiss radio. "These are public assets, not just any money."

If adopted, the fund could draw on around seven billion Swiss francs ($4.7 billion) in official gold reserves and generate several hundred million francs (dollars) a year for needy recipients in Switzerland and abroad, Koller said.

They could include "victims of poverty and catastrophes, of genocide and other serious human rights abuses, of course also for those of the Holocaust and Shoa," he said in Berne's boldest response yet to charges the Swiss coldly profited from the war.

Koller reaffirmed neutral Switzerland's commitment to facing its history squarely as it reexamines its past and urged its critics to give a historians' panel conducting a sweeping historical review the time it needs to do its job properly.
But Koller also made clear Berne felt the need to affirm Switzerland's humanitarian traditions and its thanks that it was spared the misery of two devastating wars.

"In this sense the Federal Council (cabinet), in accord with the Swiss National Bank and with an eye on the anniversary year of 1998, has developed the idea of a Swiss Foundation for Solidarity," Koller said, referring to the 150th anniversary of the modern Swiss state next year.

If the plan is adopted, the government would not contribute any public funds to a Holocaust memorial fund, something nationalist politicians have attacked as tantamount to an admission of guilty behaviour during the war.
Big Swiss banks last month donated 100 million francs ($67 million) to such a fund after being stung by accusations that they had hoarded accounts left by Holocaust victims.
The Swiss National Bank (SNB), which has acknowledged buying looted gold from Nazi Germany, also intends to contribute 100 million francs, Koller said.

SNB Chairman Hans Meyer said the new plan entailed selling gold over a 10-year period, but insisted such sales -- worth "several billion" Swiss francs -- would not have to disrupt the gold market and would not undermine the franc's stability.
He said the foundation would be financed by a substantial proportion of profits achieved by revaluing gold the central bank now has on its books at less than a third of market prices.
The SNB's 2,600 tonnes of gold -- some one percent of global annual gold output -- is valued at just under 12 billion francs at the fixed legal parity of 4,595.74 francs per kg.
